utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Wednesday, I'd like to say good morning to the witness, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, and the accused. Ladies and gentlemen, before I give the floor to Mr. Scott to continue the proceedings the registrar is going to give us some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is a new English translation of Article 34 of P 00588. That shall be given Exhibit number IC 451. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Praljak. Sir, we'll try to finish up the Prosecution's direct examination hopefully in a few minutes. What I'd like to do now is, as we mentioned in court in the last couple of days, is to show you some of the binders of the -- really all of the binders that we have been using with you or referring to in the course of your testimony. A number of the documents that we have looked at in the course of your testimony in the last two days are the type of document indicated or -- excuse me -- included in the binders. However, I'm now going to go through these binders with you in some -- slightly more detail. If I could please first of all have the witness shown binder number 1 or bundle 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sometimes -- sometimes the bundle numbers and the binder numbers, Your Honour, are not exactly the same, and that might lead to some confusion. I'll try to do the best to keep it straight. Binder 1 is in fact the same as bundle 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, based upon your having looked at that document and as you looked at that bundle of documents over the weekend, I'm going to ask you, could you please confirm to the Judges that this bundle 1 is a set of release orders signed by Stanko Bozic, the schedule beginning with Exhibit 2289, P 02289, and continuing on until P 08216. Just so the record is clear, not consecutive. The numbers are not consecutive because they are pulled from other lists, but just by way of reference the schedule begins with P 02289 and ends with P 08216. Mr. Praljak, can you just confirm that that -- the binder that is now in front of you, which is bundle 1, contains release orders signed by Mr. Bozic, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. If we could shall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one precision. Signed by Mr. Bozic or by the witness himself? Because there's some like that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Signed -- either signed -- prepared for Mr. Bozic's signature, that is the type signature, typed name, if you will, but either signed by Mr. Bozic himself or signed by the witness, Mr. Praljak. Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in that same -- in that same binder there's a divider and then you should get to bundle number 2. So again it's in -- it's in binder 1, but we're now going to bundle 2, separate schedule. And can you please confirm -- and this is the schedule that begins with -- excuse me a moment. This binder contains -- or bundle contains starting with P 02217 and the schedule ends with P 07152. These are release orders signed by either Mr. Zvonko Vidovic or Josip Marcinko. Mr. Praljak, can you confirm that is the case, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We can put up -- that binder away, please, just to avoid confusion. Next -- the next binder would be -- I'm going to do them in a group of -- I was going to do binder number 5, actually. Hold on one moment, please. I'm jumping to binder -- bundle 5. I'll come back to bundles 3 and 4 in a moment because I think some of the bundles are more directly related to each other than others. Sir, this is -- I've now put in front you -- or had put in front of you bundle number 5. These -- this is a binder containing 20 items. The schedule begins with number P 03200 continuing to P 07152 -- or again not continuing but ending with that exhibit number. These are releases signed by Mr. Berislav Pusic, and can you confirm that that's the contents of bundle number 5?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to next be shown, please, binder number 6, which is also -- binder number 6, which is also in binder 4. This is set of 12 documents. The first exhibit number in this bundle be Exhibit P 02267, the last exhibit included in this bundle being P 02476, and these are various release orders and requests signed by miscellaneous persons as listed on the description of the document, and can be just confirm -- Excuse me. Can you confirm for us, Mr. Praljak, that that is the case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can please do exhibit -- next exhibit bundle number 11 which is there binder 12 and following separately. Binder 12, bundle 11. This is schedule of 27 items. The first exhibit listed in the schedule is Exhibit P 02258 continuing to -- or the last exhibit listed being P 08773. The category or description of this particular set of 27 documents are various lists of detainees at the Heliodrom. And looking at the dates, all primarily during 1993, a few subsequent to that. Can you confirm, Mr. Praljak, please, that bundle 11 contains the material that I've just described?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I should say in general on these bundles, and when I'm asking you these questions, these are all documents of a type or form of document that you saw being used in the administration of the Heliodrom prison during the 1993, 1994 time period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I please ask you next to look at bundle number 12, which is in binder 12. This is a list of 45 items. The schedule starts with Exhibit number P 07340. The last item listed in this schedule is Exhibit P 08216. And these are documents -- these are reports on numbers of detainees kept and released from the Heliodrom during the later period December 1993 to April 1994. And again, Mr. Praljak, in looking at those and having looked at those previous to today, can you confirm that the contents of bundle 12 is as I've described it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, the reasons that I have ground bundles 1, 2, 5, 6, 11, 12 is that these are all binders dealing with lists of detainees and releases in particular in that category. If I could next ask the witness to be shown bundle number 3, which I understand extends over binders 2 and 3 but we're looking at binder -- excuse me, bundle 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Bundle 3 is a list of 262 documents. The first exhibit on the schedule being P 02667, and the last exhibit listed in this schedule being P 07091, and the category of these documents are orders for the use of detainees for labour, primarily from Mijo Jelic. And once again, Mr. Praljak, can you confirm that the documents that are contained in bundle 3 are -- are of the category that I've just described?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next please ask the witness to look at binder number 4 -- or -- my apology, bundle 4, which is in binder 4. Bundle 4 is a set of 87 items. The schedule begins with Exhibit number 02727, and the schedule ends with Exhibit number P 07459. This is a set of materials described as requests for prisoners for labour, primarily coming from Mile Puljic. Not entirely but primarily, as you look through the list, anyone will see that he is the primary person in these lists asking for prisoners for labour. And, sir, if you can look just to see again, confirm once again what you've seen in that binder 4 and that bundle 4, are those documents as I've described them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to next look at bundle number 7 which is included in binders 5 and 6. Bundle 7 is a large bundle of 337 items. The schedule begins with Exhibit number P 04898 and continues to -- or again the schedule ends with Exhibit P 07127. Excuse me, P 07127. And this document consists of approvals for taking detainees for labour. Again, 337 items, approvals to take prisoners to work. And, Mr. Praljak, can I again ask you to confirm, having reviewed these documents, that those -- the documents in bundle 7 are as I've just described them?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Going to bundle number 8, which is in binder 7. Bundle 8. Bundle 8 is a set of 118 items, 118 items the schedule beginning with P 03293, and the scheduling ending with Exhibit P 08147. The category of items included in this bundle are reports concerning detainees being beaten, wounded or killed while performing labour. And again, Mr. Praljak, can you confirm that this bundle of materials, bundle number 8, is as I've described it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going to bundle number 10, which is in binders -- these logbooks that are quite thick and therefore that's the reason they are spread over bundle -- excuse me, binders 8, 9, 10, and 11. Again, bundle 10, but binders 8, 9, 10, and 11. This is a set of 13 items starting on the schedule with Exhibit P 00285 and ending with P 08202 described as logbooks and various logbooks used in the administration of the prison. Most of them -- all or most of them, one can see looking at the face of the schedule, dealing with the taking of prisoners for labour. Again, some of these we've seen in court as examples. The logbook from the prison building, the logbook from the school, and the sports hall. Sir, can you again confirm that the documents or items in bundle 10 or -- are the documents as I've described them just now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to bundle number 9, which is binder 7. Bundle 9, binder 7 is a compilation of nine items, a short set of items. The list starting with Exhibit number P 01514 and continuing to P 09121, and these are various documents written and/or signed by the witness himself which we have not specifically -- some -- at least some of which we have not specifically addressed in the course of his testimony. Sir, is it correct that bundle number 9 consists of approximately nine documents signed -- either written or signed by you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally binder -- excuse me, bundle 14, bundle 14, which is in binder 16. Did not have any particular occasion to refer to it in your testimony, but is it correct, sir, that in the course of the events in -- including 1993 that you kept a -- you kept a diary and that the original language version or a copy of the original language version of that -- of your diary and an English translation is included in bundle 14?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand this was for whatever reason previously listed at one time as part of bundle 9, but in any event, it is -- the diary is more specifically Exhibit P 00352. So in this instance the exhibit number and the bundle and the content is one and the same. It's one exhibit, P 00352.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I just for the record so there is no confusion, I have not mentioned binder 13 or bundle 13, and that is the working bundle that we've used in the courtroom. So, Your Honour, with that -- Your Honours, with that the Prosecution has covered bundles 1 through 14 inclusive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Praljak. I just have a couple of final questions for you before concluding the direct examination. Prior to coming to The Hague were you -- did you have a conversation with anyone in the past several weeks that someone said something to you about the value of your testimony or whether you should come to The Hague or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only had a meeting with Mr. Marinko Skobic, an attorney in Mostar. The conversation did not evolve nor was anything suggested by him which would influence me as to what kind of testimony I would give.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning Your Honours. I don't believe we've received anything as far as proofing notes and I imagine this would have come out during the proofing session. I don't know where the gentleman is going. I do think this is something that should have been provided to the Defence in advance. I hope in the future this will not occur again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with Mr. Karnavas, and since the witness has already said that it did not influence him as to what kind of testimony he would give, it would appear that what he's about to say is irrelevant, as well as being a form of ambush of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As to the notice issue, Your Honour, it appears I may be in a position to owe the Defence an apology for that. And as to the item, this is the item that the witness just referred to. Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Scott. Counsel on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I feel prompted to give a brief explanation. On the 6th of March last year, I sent a letter to the Prosecution using previous practice saying that we wished to talk to some of the witnesses. We never received a response, feedback information, and Mr. Skobic is a member of the Pusic Defence team, and I think Mr. Scott can confirm that the letter was sent out and he was informed about the conversation. The witness said that there was no pressure exerted on him or any influence wielded, so I wanted to give that brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the problem with -- one of the problems with not -- attempting not to lead a witness is that there could be any number of items that the witness then might volunteer. In response to my question, the witness has just volunteered a statement about Mr. Skobic which was not the person or topic that I was inquiring about. So unfortunately I have no quarrel with what Mr. Ibrisimovic has said, but it's not concerning contact with Mr. Skobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, have you -- you're a pensioner; is that correct? You receive a pension now?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did someone that you worked with or have contact with in connection with the administration of your pension say something to you about the value of your evidence or whether you should come to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Scott is proceeding without -- without obtaining a ruling of the Trial Chamber. We have made an objection to this as being, first of all, apparently irrelevant; and secondly, a form of ambush of which we have been given no notice, and I would ask the Trial Chamber, please, to rule upon this before allowing it to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood it is the witness himself that broke the -- brought the subject up and told you that he had met with Mr. Skobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it, isn't it? And you wanted to inform the Chamber thereof, of that element.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was not clear. The question -- the topic of the question that I initiated a couple of moments ago does not involve Mr. Skobic at all, but the witness -- about Mr. Skobic. I'm talking about another situation. The contact with Mr. Skobic for our purposes is completely irrelevant. It was not the reason I was asking my question. During the course of -- if you want to -- perhaps, Your Honour, I don't want to have too much discussion of this prior to the witness -- in front of the witness, but I can tell the Chamber, if you wish, the topic of the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's put Mr. Skobic to the side. Mr. Ibrisimovic made the comments he wanted so we've dealt with the Skobic matter. Now, what was the other problem you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I wish to ask the witness, Your, Honour to confirm that the man who administers his pension told him that he really probably shouldn't come to The Hague, that he really had nothing to offer; it would not be in his interest to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, with all due respect. It seem -- I understand the Prosecution wanting to get this information out. They learned of it. Perhaps they feel an obligation to do so. However, now it's casting some negative light on the accused as if somebody is trying to get to this witness. Now -- well, you're shaking your head, Judge Trechsel, but being on the Defence side I have to wonder, you know, because it gives the impression that somehow we're trying to get to the witness. Now, I've never met the man. I don't know why this person said whatever it is. The gentleman decided to testify nonetheless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody said it was you. Why do you think so? Nobody said it was you. Now, Witness, can you explain the situation around your pension? What happened in that regard? Explain that to us, please, Witness, because we can invoke contempt of court if anybody has exerted pressure on a witness. So tell us, please, sir, what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days before I set out to testify here I was called up by the prosecutor of the Herzegovina-Neretva county Zdravko Skaric [as interpreted]. I thought he was going to say that I needed some additional papers because I am a war invalid and receive the remuneration which comes to 315 convertible marks, and I asked -- I said to him, "Why have you called me up?" He said, "I haven't got your documents here. They're in Sarajevo." And I said, "Well, what do you need the documents for, chief?" And I'm going to quote him. He said, "You're not going to help your cousin much in The Hague." And this surprised me coming from him, and I said, "I don't know the sense of that conversation. I don't know what you mean," and I left. I went out of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why -- why do we -- I can't, Your Honour. Why don't we get this information in advance? And what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in what does this concern Mr. Prlic? You are getting agitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It concerns the entire Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Oui.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. First of all, Witness, in line 2 of page 13, lines 1 and 2, there may be an error because you said you were called up by the prosecutor of this county. Mr. Skaric is in fact who? I thought it was an administrative official, not the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's not the prosecutor. It's not the prosecutor. It's a person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We call him director or, rather, deputy director for defenders of the HVO of the Herzegovina-Neretva district.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I just correct, Your Honour, for the record his name. I think it's in the record as "Skaric," which I don't believe is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you repeat the name of this person who made this comment to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdravko Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Talic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: T-a-l-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The impression that is being created is he came to see you about your pension, and he must know obviously that you are a relative of Mr. Praljak, his cousin, that you are going to The Hague and you are probably not going to do him service, a favour. So do you think he was expressing his personal sentiments or he was doing that to exert pressure on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't decide, and I couldn't think about it because I was so taken aback by what he said. And I replied, "I am an invalid, and in view of my disability, I am acquitting myself pretty well, and I know very well what I'm going to say and talk about."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, the Chamber has conferred, and we believe that this is incidental and has no bearing on the subject at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we won't go into it any further --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. The information has been provided and we will not belabour it at this point. In terms of the significance of it, Your Honour, and again I don't want to take the time now or the witness's time to go into it, the Prosecution -- the very, very short version is the Prosecution believes it's relevant to the Chamber to know the environment in which these witnesses live and come to The Hague in, and we feel it our obligation, as we have on a number of occasions, that when we receive information from a witness that a witness believes he or she has been harassed or interfered with or something untoward has been said to the witness in any way that we bring that to the attention of the Chamber. In the past number months, a number of statements have been made and claims have been made about there's no problems down there, everything is fine, and, Your Honour, that's not the Prosecution's position. And when a witness comes to us and says someone that administers his pension, his livelihood, the means that he supports himself, and makes a comment to the effect of discouraging him from coming to The Hague to give his evidence, we think that's relevant, and we will continue to bring that information before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think it would be -- it is called for that you explain to the Chamber why you did not warn the Defence in advance of this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My error, Your Honour. My error. I was here all weekend and I didn't do it. I've been working and Ms. Egels, non-stop. I apologise. I apologise to the Defence. It probably won't be the first it probably won't be the last, Your Honour, but it was my oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Shouldn't the consequence then be that you forget about this point and not bring it up? I think that would be the full respect of fairness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I respectfully submit that is not to do with these charges.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's going on and off, Your Honour. With all respect, Judge Trechsel, I don't believe so. Granted it has nothing to do with the counts of the indictment per se but it is conduct related to a witness that they think the Chamber should be aware of. Again I extend my apology. I'm not here to provide any other excuse except it was oversight, unfortunately. The Prosecution team is working very hard. I personally worked 14 hours on Sunday from 8.30 in the morning until 10.30 Sunday night, and I forgot. I forgot and I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, just a few seconds. You know that there is a rule concerning contempt of court, and persons shall be responsible for contempt of court if they tamper with the administration of justice and if they are guilty of any failure to present relevant evidence. So you are, together with your colleagues, entitled to make an inquiry in this case. That is your role. There is a rule in the Rules of Procedure that allows you to take such a step and to act upon that rather than on theories and hypotheses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to belabour it any further and take the Court's time or my time to do it this morning, but I think that -- I think it is relevant for the Chamber to know whether contempt charges are ever brought or not the Chamber is entitled to be informed of the environment in which the case proceeds. Whether we can prove a contempt case against any particular individual or not or whether it warrants an actual prosecution or not are separate decisions but the Chamber, in our respectful decision, should have the information and when we talk about protective measures and that sort of thing that the witnesses who come here, the Chamber needs to be fully advised as to the situation in that regard. Now, let me just say to conclude this that there is one other matter about a contact with this witness but in light of what's been said this morning we'll make a separate filing of that, but in this particular case I must advise the Chamber, I have to advise the Chamber in case the Chamber wants to inquire of the witness, but in this case it was a contact directly by one of the accused in this case, and I'll leave it at that. If the Chamber wants to inquire, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the microphones aren't -- Your Honour, this is absolutely disgraceful. And I've known Mr. Scott there the beginning of this case and I have implicit faith in him personally but this is absolutely disgraceful. The Prosecution here is -- is trying to poison the mind of the Trial Chamber with innuendo and rumour without actually bringing it to the attention of the Defence so that it can be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Murphy. The word "to poison" was already used in written submissions, and we have already replied that the minds of the Judges cannot be poisoned. A Judge cannot be poisoned in his mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to hear that, Your Honour, and I -- I -- as you know I have the utmost confidence in the Trial Chamber, but the point that the Prosecution should not be making the attempt to do it. Now, we've -- it's happened time after time, as Your Honour knows in this trial, that a witness comes to The Hague and says something to the Prosecution about some contact that's been made and the immediate reaction is the Prosecution applies for protective measures. And then we have a discussion about that and they're either granted or refused. Are now, this information was available to the Prosecution. If -- if there was a good faith concern about it they had ample time to make a filing and to advise the Defence that they were seeking protective measures for the witness which would have taken care of the situation. This has not been done. And what's happening now is that by innuendo, again, we're hearing that contacts are being made, things are going on back there. The intent -- the intent being to suggest something nefarious without committing themselves to any specific allegations and now we're ambushed. We don't have the time to deal with it. We were not given notice. Your Honour, the -- this is an unacceptable situation. If this -- if the Defence did things like this we would be in serious trouble, and there should not be a double standard for the Prosecution. This is an outrage. I protest against it, and I ask that the Prosecution be admonished and instructed not to take this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I briefly -- briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You have to allow me to respond. Those are strong statements. With all respect, Your Honour, please, allow a very brief response. First of all, the witness did not seek protective measures. It's his prerogative to ask but he thought and we thought that the information should be provided to the Chamber whether he seeks protective measures in this case or not. A witness may be very robust in his case and decide, I don't want protective measures. I want to give my testimony publicly. But at the same time at the same time I want the Chamber to be informed of this information and it still remains the Prosecution's position that the Chamber is entitled to the information. I have offered my apology. I did not duck the issue. I offer no excuse other than oversight on my part for which I apologise to the Chamber and to counsel but sometimes mistakes do happen unfortunately. That is a reality, and I think it's -- I have a great respect for Mr. Murphy, who I consider my friend, but some of the statements he has just made I believe are over -- over the top. As to the second item, Your Honour, I will not proceed further again except to respond to counsel's comments. This is not innuendo. This witness, the man sitting here had face-to-face contact with one of the accused in this case. There is no innuendo whatsoever. He can tell you about it under oath right here. He can tell you who he talked to but I leave it in the Chamber's hands. There is no innuendo at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, it seems that you had a conversation with one of the accused. Is that right or not? What can you tell us? Did you speak to your cousin if it's your cousin? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was last year. I was shopping when I got a call from the brother of Mr. Berko Pusic. Together with my wife I went into his office and there I met with Mr. Berko Pusic. I was surprised. Both my wife and I exchanged courtesies with him. There was not much talk between us. He did not tell me anything in the sense that I should change anything to my testimony or statements, and at that time I didn't even know that I would be called here as a witness. So we stayed there very briefly, said our good-byes, and my wife and I went home. That was my entire contact with Mr. Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So you did not speak about the substance of this case. It was a purely friendly meeting, an encounter among friends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The only thing is that in that conversation I just said, "Berko, in case I am invited to The Hague, I will tell only the truth." He only answered, "All right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This incident is closed. We move to the Defence now. It's 10 -- or, rather, it's a quarter to 10.00. It's time to start the cross-examination. Who will start?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will start. May I ask the usher, and I didn't have occasion to do that before, to take this bundle of documents. Your Honour, I don't want to deal any more with these issues because you have closed the discussion, although it does upset me a little in the beginning of my cross-examination in view of this information which just heard. I would have much preferred if we had received it earlier, speaking on behalf of the Stojic Defence. If we had occasion to know this before, we would have inquired into the identity of that person who spoke to the witness, because it seems to be some sort of deputy director, which in our system is not supposed to hand out pensions, and we would have been able to show that this pressure, if any, is certainly not one that was exerted by our clients. But I hope that in the future we will receive this kind of information in good time and thus be able to assist the Court in clearing up anything that needs to be cleared up and is vague.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You just received a bundle of documents from me, but you don't have to look at them now. And the usher didn't need to stay there either. I was informed that a new system was being introduced with regard to the presentation of documents, so I prepared hard copies for the ELMO should we have any problems. Now, with regard to the last point that the Prosecutor raised with you, I think that through these bundles of documents the Prosecutor questioned you as to whether you had reviewed all of the documents contained therein, and I'd like to ask you how much time did you spend in proofing with the Prosecutor, and how much time in total did you have to review the documents in all these binders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent the whole day of Saturday, from morning to the evening, and the whole day on Sunday, as well as Monday until 12.30. For three days I didn't go out anywhere. I just reviewed the documents. I even had lunch here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I believe my colleagues will deal with it as well, but let me ask you, do you know how many documents in total are contained in the binders that you say you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I leafed through all of them but I didn't count them. I didn't bother.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the record I'll say that there are 1.344 documents there. You say, and I take your word for it, I have no reason not to, that you reviewed all of them, and that on top of that you had enough time to speak to the Prosecutor about specific documents.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one clarification. Since the documents are divided by categories, and if they relate to Mr. Mijo Jelic, all the documents were in the possession of Mijo Jelic in the same format, with the same signature, and if they were not signed by him they were signed by his deputy, Vladimir Primorac Dedo, or alternatively Ivica Cavar. Another category from the 3rd Brigade is also of the same format, along the same lines, filled in in the same way, signed by Pavlovic or Mile Pusic or Pajo Sopta. So it was much easier to go through those documents than if they had been all heaped together. Then I wouldn't have managed to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the transcript. But you will agree with me that although one person signed them, all different context. You just explained how you managed to review them quickly without going into the substance because they were all from one person. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it exactly the same way, but being familiar with a document from 1993, I knew where my eyes need to go and what I need to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I don't want to dwell on it any further. We'll see later through the documents that I will present to you to what extent you really are familiar with some of those documents. Please, on the 1st of July, 1992, did you start working at the district prison in Mostar? And did the warden of that prison tell you on your very first day that you would be overseeing works to convert the building at Heliodrom, that should become a military investigations prison or a military prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before the works began did you make a sketch of the premises in that building that needed to be converted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day or the next day, it's in my diary, we went down there accompanied by a gentleman who knew the location, Mr. Nikola Puce, and who took me there to show me which building was selected so that I made that sketch. In fact, I made the layout of the building to facilitate making a specification of the material that needed to go into that building. Because that was a school. It was full of some material in the basement, infantry equipment. People were getting trained there. All that needed to be removed and cleaned and cleared up, and then only start works.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript so we don't overlap. Can you tell me, was that the building that on the layout shown you by the Prosecutor under IC number 449 you designated as the prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at the entry in diary for the 2nd of July, 1992. It's P 00352. So that you don't have to look for it, I'll ask the usher to give it to you. I prepared it because it would have taken you a long time to find it, together with the layout. We'll use the layout later, but now look in your diary, page for the 1st of July. It's the next page, the next one after this. In English it's page 3. And in the Croatian version it's marked 03540172. This is the ERN number. It's your entry for the 1st of July. You have probably found it by now; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You say somewhere in the middle that it was your first day at work, that you were given the responsibility to carry out these works; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's just look at page 3 in English, the entry for the next day. Is that the layout we are discussing now? So in English page 3. In Croatian it's 0354. One page further, please. Could the usher please -- no, in fact, the usher didn't need to stand by the witness at this moment. If we could just place the proper page in e-court. That's much more important now. I believe the Judges have found the page showing a layout of the first floor and the stairwell. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is this first floor? Next page. Next page. Could you tell us in your own words what is depicted here? We see three rooms of 3 by 5.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here the ground floor, the official entrance, service entrance, into the building on the ground floor. This is a hallway that on the right-hand side had a room of 3 by 5. That's 15 square metres. And we had to mark the area in order to know the whole area of the building so that we can make a specification for later works.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page? This was the first floor. In English it's page 4. We see the ground floor and the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we go upstairs, up these stairs, what is depicted here is just one side of the floor, the right side where bars were put up, which means that all these rooms beyond the dotted line were separated from the staircase and that area was under lock with the key in the possession of the shift commander. There was one bedroom, later turned into a bedroom, in fact, 60 square metres. Second bedroom or dormitory, 97 square metres, and a third one of an area of 45 square metres. And what we see over here were the bathroom and the lavatory with showers and four or five toilets. And the running water was available throughout. This same layout was on the other side, on the left side. So it was not shown. And the dimensions are the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Now, can we then conclude that what you've just described to us is the first floor and that you had running water, enough hot water, but tell us what happened on the ground floor. What was the situation like on the ground floor that you put there? Ground floor.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ground floor here as shown was the same thing, the same distribution and layout of the rooms. There was this same thing on the ground floor, which means the same number of rooms as on the floor above.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Over the next few days in your diary you say that the work was progressing satisfactorily, and we can see from your diary that you were receiving the necessary material for the adaptation and that the whole adaptation was completed with people moving in on the 22nd of September, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In your diary you also say how you procured the equipment after having taken up accommodation in the premises. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's see what your entry was for the 24th of September, for instance. And I'd like to emphasise that in the English version it is on page 15. Have you found that? Tell me when you find it. I'm referring to your entry of the 24th of September. The ERN number is 03540184. And I said that in English it was on page 13. Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 24th of September. You've found it. Right. Now, here we see that you have a meeting with the warden for that day, and the first thing says: "Urgently to see to the telephones," but we're not going to deal with that in the prison. But then you say: "The warden gave permission for five people for tomorrow to buy covers, blankets, and so on." Then it says that some people worked on digging up the potatoes. And may we have a look at the next page. It's page 16 in the English. And the note for the 26th of September, let's look at that -- or, rather, the 27th of September where you say that you had a meeting with the warden and that the warden gave permission for six people to move the furniture. And then underneath that we see that on the 28th of September the warden ordered the warehouse clerk, Andjelko Filipovic, to construct some cupboards for the kitchen. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, from this logbook or diary of yours we can see that for the most part you managed during that time of adaptation to obtain all the necessary material for this facility to function. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So the facility then, once people had moved into it, can we say that it satisfied requirements, fully satisfied the needs and requirements necessary for, as you said, putting up 500 to 550 detainees?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this was a premises that had been adapted to be used in this way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, can you tell me whether around the facility that we refer to as the prison, the prison proper, was there a wire fence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was that wire fence put up?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was down there it hadn't been put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there an entrance gate in front of the facility?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no gate. There was just a large metal door on the facility itself, but before that there was no gate. It was only later on towards the end of 1993 when the prisoner of war shelter had been put up that the wire fence had been put up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This shelter or accommodation that you said was erected later on and had this wire fence, did it incorporate this building, too, the building that you prepared and adapted for being the central investigating prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we now look at the layout of the Heliodrom barracks and it is document P 09219 [as interpreted]. May we have the sketch put up on the ELMO, please. I have provided the sketch. The witness has it. It is document -- while we're waiting for it to come up on the ELMO, or we can all take a look at it on the ELMO. Did you place your signature to this sketch as well as the date in the upper right-hand corner? And when did you do that, if you did?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did this during my work with the investigators, and once again confirmed it on Saturday when I came on Saturday or Sunday and went through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you happen to notice that on the sketch it says that it is an HVO concentration camp named Heliodrom? Look at what it says at the top as a heading. It says the "plan of the former JNA barracks and HVO concentration camp Heliodrom."

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading that now but I didn't notice it earlier on. I wasn't paying attention to what it said as a heading. All I did was to look at the sketch and the layout and be able to mark what I had been asked to mark, the places where the prison was and which facilities were used. But let me say straight away that I do not agree as a witness, and I would never have used this term "concentration camp." I would never have used that expression because I wasn't marking concentration camps. All I was doing was marking facilities where the prisoners of war were held captive as well as military prisoners and detainees.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleagues have drawn my attention to the fact that it's the wrong exhibit on e-court. But let's forget the e-court. We have the proper document on the overhead projector that we're discussing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to clarify with you, sir, because it would emerge from this that you put your signature and date to a document which I assume because you spent so much time working there and trying to put things the way they should be that you would never accept that this is a concentration camp. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I as a witness do not wish to utter that word ever. I don't want that word to come out of my mouth ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, with the explanation that we have been given along with this sketch I would like to ask you now to use your marker to draw a circle around the building which you adapted and which, in fact, was the prison building once it had been adapted. So would you draw a circle around that building, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Draw a circle round the building.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, as being the building that you had adapted. Thank you. My colleague is drawing my attention to the fact that the document number is 09121. I think that's what I said. And we should be able to see the number on the ELMO. The number is P 09121. That is the correct number for the transcript. And I'd like to ask you to sign your name, and I'd like an IC number for this sketch, because the witness has indicated only the facility that was used as the prison.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 452, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now would we -- I would like us to focus on the area which you in police jargon or used by people working in the prison, the area that is referred to as solitary confinement cells. You can leave the sketch behind and just listen to me. Tell me where these solitary confinement cells were on this layout.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The solitary confinement cells were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Had those premises been renovated too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, those premises have not been drawn into the layout that we look out in your logbook for the 2nd of July, 1992. They weren't drawn in there, were they?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this was in the basement, which is where the dining-room was as well as the kitchen and the warehouse and the other storage spaces. So I didn't draw in anything there. And it was all adapted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think that the usher can go back to his seat. We won't be needing his services until the break, so not to keep him standing. Now, when you say that -- when you say that this part had been adapted, did it have the furniture and everything necessary?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention, sir, to something related to the solitary confinement cells and the general conditions that prevailed in Heliodrom, because I want through you -- I want you to assist us and to assist the Court and the Trial Chamber in the first place, to clarify certain matters because some witnesses testified about these things, and that's why I'm asking you about them. Tell me, please, when you say that the solitary confinement cells were furnished, can you remember how large these rooms were and what the furnishings were once the adaptation had been completed? Were there -- was there a water installation system and so on?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The solitary confinement cells within the prison did not have -- well, there weren't -- there wasn't much difference from the solitary confinement cells there compared to the solitary cells in the Ricinova Street prison. And that building in Ricinova Street existed previously in the system, and so we were guided by this in order to make these confinement cells similar to the ones that existed in that other building. And each cell in the basement in that part of the building had daylight, light coming in from outside. They had a door, half with bars, which means that you could see through those bars, and the lower part of the door was closed. Inside the cells there was nothing except something for sleeping on, and that was a sponge mattress. There were no beds. So sponge and covering. As far as the water installation, there was no water in the cell, but at all times the guard who was in that area could be called by the prisoner and taken to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Some witnesses said that their -- that some people had beds but that others slept on the floor with the sponges. So I want to ask you whether there were any beds in the solitary confinement cells when the facility opened.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the very beginning, the cells were made the way they would have been made in peacetime, and those facilities, which means that there were sponges, sponge mattresses, and some cells had beds too. At that time you can rest assured that everything was done by the book, as the provisions stated for solitary confinement cells.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I think that you've said something very important for the Trial Chamber to know. You worked in the Ricinova Street in the civilian prison there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you know the standards that prevailed for those facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you said that once the adaptation of the solitary confinement cells were constructed they were identical to standard of cell and standard of prisoners in solitary confinement cells that existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in Heliodrom in the military investigation cell, the cells were in fact larger, taking the square metres, than the cells were in Ricinova Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that the guard that was on duty there would allow prisoners from time to time when they needed to, to go to the toilet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How -- what about the other hygiene conditions? Could the prisoners go escorted by the guard to the bathrooms that were up on the floor above?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this was all regulated and agreed upon in the building, and everything depended on the guard, whether the guard would fulfil his duties or not. Am I understanding you correctly on that point?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we now focus on the period of time that is interesting to me. Although I'd like to go into all the details, of course, and see what you have to say, but I would like us to try and focus now on the period after the 30th of June, because that's when most of the witnesses -- that's the period that most of the witnesses testified about. Now, in that period after the 30th of June, who was in those confinement cells? How many people were confined in solitary confinement cells? Were they overcrowded, and can you tell us something about that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 30th of June when the detainees started to arrive in large numbers the building began to fill up and the building became full. And once it was full, somebody allowed the others, the rest of the detainees, to be placed in the school building and sports halls.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Excuse me, but we've heard all that, all of it. I just want you to focus on these pages. Who, after the 30th of June, to the best your knowledge, was placed on these premises? We know the rest.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the isolation cells there were people, all those that the SIS service or the crime prevention service sent to the isolation cells for the duration of interrogation of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, we could say that those were people who were under investigation in a way. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under investigation, because that was in the jurisdiction of the SIS and the crime prevention service. Officers from those two services could order that somebody be placed in an isolation cell or removed from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it was their decision. You and the warden had no say in it, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. We had no say in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me who kept those rooms clean?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean who purchased the material or who --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. I mean who kept them clean? Who did the actual cleaning? I'm asking this because some witnesses earlier spoke of very poor hygienic conditions, and as my colleague says, we might be able to get step-by-step who was in charge of what.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cleaning was done by the prisoners, block by block. The isolation cells were cleaned by those who were inside. That's how it worked from day-to-day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If I can just rephrase what you just said. In every section of the building, in every block the prisoners from that block did the cleaning.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because in every section one of the prisoners was a liaison with the guard in charge of that block. He would request all the material, and he would organise the cleaning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Some of the witnesses stated that these rooms were full of water, that prisoners had to go to the toilet in buckets that were not emptied regularly. Do you know anything about that, and do you know who was able to order or organise that this water be removed and that hygienic conditions be improved?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners could only have claimed that about the period when the prison was overcrowded and maybe the isolation cells were full at that time. Otherwise, in every other period every prisoner who felt the need to go to the toilet and couldn't wait for a guard to take him out could avail himself of the bucket that was in the isolation cell in order to avoid doing it on the floor. Afterwards, he would call the guard and the guard would help him take the bucket out and escort him back to the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As an employee of the prison, sir, have you ever visited the prison in Zenica which is still one of the most important prisons in the federation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wanted to, but I never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would have liked to compare the hygienic conditions in the isolation cells there and in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they also had the same kind of buckets like in the military prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that surprises me a little, the way you describe hygienic conditions. If there was water on the floor, maybe something was out of order, some sort of installation was broken. Were you able or maybe the warden was able to deal with breakdowns, with things that needed to be repaired, because that, if true, would have really soured the life of all those people who were there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing of anything like it. At the prison we also had the so-called housekeeper who was able to perform any repairs on the plumbing, and that would have been done immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I just have two or three more questions before the break on this topic. You had insight. You were able to see the conditions. It wasn't something that you were not able to see for yourself and organise or order to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, until the 30th of June, inside the prison itself everything was -- or could be perfectly under control and everything would function well. However, when we had that large influx of people, of course the hygiene deteriorated due to overcrowding.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you this question for a purpose, because I wanted to assist the Court. It's clear that things changed in the later period. You said the general standards declined, there was overcrowding, and the hygiene suffered. But still, do you believe that the living conditions were tolerable in terms of hygiene? We'll talk about food later.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to say one thing. To keep things clean, every day, 24 hours a day, there was running water at the prison. Prisoners could take showers and baths, and nobody kept them away from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Including those in the isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including those in the isolation cells. They just had to ask the policeman standing outside the cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. Some former inmates said that they had been concealed from the ICRC before the ICRC would come for a visit. In fact, they said they were taken to some sort of cinema hall from the isolation cells prior to ICRC visits.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The ICRC actually came for the first time on the 10th of August after this large influx of new inmates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's on the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you had no knowledge that anybody concealed people held in isolation cells? It would have been an order that had to come down from the warden, so you would have known about it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the clock, Your Honour. I have completed this subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll go on a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Witness, I have before me a report of the Spanish delegation to the European mission that sometime around 4 to 9 September visited Heliodrom. Were you present during their visit to Heliodrom in 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. If my name was there, then I was there. If not, then I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll just ask you about one small detail. It says in the report that at that time, that means September 1993, prisoners had just installed central heating themselves. Do you remember central heating in one of the buildings in Heliodrom at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you tell me how many meals prisoners got every day? I am referring throughout to the period after the 30th of June, but with regard to meals can you also cover the period from the 9th of May onwards and the prisoners to got there on the 9th of May and stayed till the end? Was there any difference in the meals, and how many meals per day were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to answer that question for one particular reason, namely a large influx of prisoners meant that it was not possible to plan for the central kitchen to make that many meals for the newly arrived prisoners, thus the logistical component envisaged metal lunchboxes with biscuits at times when it was not possible to make meals. Those who had just arrived and could not receive a meal from the central kitchen received a biscuit from those metal boxes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mean to say that such occurrences could last for a day or two but not longer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the next day Mr. Bozic would not know exactly how many prisoners there were inside, but he took a number that he could provide for, and then again a new cycle would begin. New arrivals would get biscuits until the next day when meals could be ordered for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me to the best of your recollection about the longest period, apart from those days which were exceptions, how many meals per day did prisoners receive?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to receive three meals a day, but I would say that there was not a single day when they did not get at least two.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That is precisely what this report of the Spanish delegation, dated 14th of September, says. Some of prior witnesses said that for the duration of their stay at Heliodrom lost up to a half of their body weight. For instance, from the 30th of June until the end of the year, some of them said they lost 40 to 50 kilos. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it. And I'm surprised, because everybody who got there, including the Red Cross, failed to make such an observation. I don't think I can agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, did all the inmates get the same food? I mean all of them in all the three buildings, and especially the one called "Prison," in all of its sections, the isolation cells, the section of the first floor, the section for civilians, and the section for women? Did they get all the same meals?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about the poor hygienic conditions that prisoners from Dretelj were subjected to.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us now to what extent hygienic conditions were objectively better and to what extent let's say the category of prisoners of war were better nourished and better off? Do you think the conditions were really much better in Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging from what the prisoners themselves said, the ones who came from Dretelj and the way they appeared, it seemed that Heliodrom was a hotel for them. And there was a book that one Muslim man wrote while at Heliodrom in which I read about this one detail, and I saw it on television too. That man said and wrote, "When I came to Heliodrom, it was like coming home." So in their own words, when they saw running water they said, "We can't believe our eyes."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Of course the sight of water must have been pleasing to anyone, but it was not only water, was it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're overlapping. You're overlapping. Witness, you must wait some time after the lawyer has terminated before you reply, because otherwise the interpreters simply cannot follow, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I was actually expecting praise from you at the beginning -- at the end of my cross-examination, because I'm really trying so hard for the record to be clear, but it still does happen sometimes. I will ask the witness to pay attention too. This information about the name of this man is rather important for me. Could we move into private session for a moment so that the witness can tell me his name? It seems rather important to me because the witness is invoking a source?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure I'll be able to provide you with the name in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, did you know or were aware of that anybody during that period of time when you worked at Heliodrom, which is the relevant material time, that anybody abused or mistreated the detainees?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I didn't know about that, and if I had, I would have written it down.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. And to follow on from what you said and what you noticed as the warden or deputy warden or commander, you wrote letters to people. So I assume that had you had that kind of information you would have either written it down in your own diary and logbook or you would have written a letter to someone about it. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote were reports, or I could convey what I had heard orally, or I might have heard it from a warden or a police member or a member of the army if I had heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, had there been any abuse of detainees or detainees with any visible injuries, would you have been duty-bound to investigate and to establish who was responsible and then called for either criminal proceedings to be initiated or an inquiry or something like that? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise for insisting, but I really do have to insist on this. So you say that information of that kind that things like that were going on was something you did not have? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know anything about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bozic ever speak to you of things like that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let me ask you a hypothetical question. Had things like that been going on, would Mr. Bozic have had to know about it? Would those on guard duty have to write reports of that kind, and did the detainees have any contact with Mr. Bozic? I gather that they didn't have direct contact with you, but did they have direct contact and communication with Mr. Bozic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that Mr. Bozic from time to time would tour the premises and talk to the prisoners. Now, everything about what had happened between 6.00 p.m. until the following morning, reports about that would be brought in by Ante Smiljanic. Now, if Ante Smiljanic as a commander of the shift brought in information like that, then Bozic would have known about it. If no report was submitted to that effect, then Bozic could not have known about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ante Smiljanic was duty-bound I assume to record any goings-on like that, because if he had knowledge of things like that happening without recording them and then Mr. Bozic learned about that later on, then it would have been Mr. Smiljanic who be held responsible; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the shift duty that was on that night conveyed something like that to Ante Smiljanic and without Mr. Ante Smiljanic reporting on to Mr. Bozic, then it would Mr. Ante Smiljanic who would be held responsible for withholding information.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Since you say that you had no information to that effect, would it be right to say that to your knowledge things like that did not happen? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to move on now to another area very briefly and look at documents presented to you by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before I do that I would like to inform Their Honours that before the break, as I was informed by the registrar, that I had used up 45 minutes. Now, since I have one hour and 30 minutes and have been given approximately 30 minutes more from Counsel Alaburic, or, rather, the Petkovic Defence, I have a total of one hour and 15 minutes left during this session, and I'll do my best to finish a little before that because the other Defence teams need time for the cross-examination too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, the Prosecution showed you P 00677 yesterday. We can have it shown on e-court, because it will take too much time for you to find it in your binder, and I'm sure you'll recall the document. May we have it up on e-court, Prosecution exhibit. Here it is. You can see what this is about. You've already looked at it. It is a report on the release of prisoners on the 30th of October, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You confirms that this is a report, for the record, by Mr. Valentin Coric sent to Mr. Bruno Stojic in which he informs him that in keeping with the agreement reached with the representatives of the International Red Cross, the EC monitors, UNPROFOR, and from an order issued by the chief of the defence department of the 20th of October, 1992, all war prisoners were unconditionally released from the military remand centres in Livno, Mostar, and Tomislavgrad on the 30th of October, 1992. And you confirm that you know about this and that you were even present when these people were lined up and released. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, take a look at my binder and find the following document to look at Mr. Bruno Stojic's order to clear that up, to see what it was like, and why this release came about. So would you look at Exhibit -- well, it's in the Prosecution binder again. It is P 00665. P 00665 is the document number. Let's take a look at what it says. It's an order from Mr. Bruno Stojic where he says that from the military investigation prison, the HVO, that unconditionally all prisoners of war should be released who were held by the HVO. Now let's look at the reasons. In conformity with the agreement reached with the representatives of the International Red Cross, the EEC monitors, and UNPROFOR -- I don't intend to read this whole order, but we can see clearly that the order was issued by Mr. Bruno Stojic, and we can see the reason for which it was issued and that this made it incumbent upon Mr. Valentin Coric to implement this order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On e-court, please, and you can look at my pink binder or you can use e-court, whichever you like, but the document is 2D 00417 that I'd like to look at next so that we can see the reason for the release or, rather, on what grounds Mr. Stojic was able to issue this order, and I think you'll be able to assist us in the matter, and I'm sure you'll remember the circumstances underlying this next document. 2D 00417 is the document number. Are there any problems? Can you find it? Perhaps you can find it in your pink binder too. It says 00417 at the top of the page. It's a small piece of paper, and the usher will help you out. And here we have it up on our screens on e-court. Perhaps that's easier for you. Take a look at the document. It is a document of the -- can we see the top of the document?
