It is a document of the International Red Cross committee, and it says: "Regarding our discussion at Geneva on October 15, 1992, during the meeting with Humanitarian Issues Group at the international conference," it says, "I wish to inform you on the following," and then we have the text, and the entire text says that each party is duty-bound to release prisoners, and the international -- as soon as the International Red Cross asks for it in compliance with the plan on prisoners release and transfer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. It is only a technical matter as far as the translation of this letter is concerned that now we are speaking -- I mean, in the English translation there is "Mr. Ogata," but she was Mrs. Ogata, that is the High Commissioner for Refugees, and then it should be taken that we are talking about Madam Ogata, who was Japanese, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, you noticed that obvious mistake. But I'm looking at the original. It says Mrs. Sadako Ogata, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we have an agreement here on the release of all prisoners -- or, rather, all prisoners. It says "all prisoners." And that's what it says, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In our translation it says "civilians." And I think also in -- in the original version it is talk of [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's okay. But precisely because it reference to civilians as well, it says, yes, "the release of all civilians who had been detained by all the conflicting parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina and their return to their homes in compliance with Article 3, paragraph 2 of the agreement accepted by all three sides at Geneva. All three sides are duty-bound to release the prisoners as soon as the ICRC asks for it in compliance with the plan on prisoners' release and transfer. Each side to release their prisoners." Yes, Your Honour, it says civilians, but later on it says prisoners near too.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would like you to confirm, Witness, if this relates to the Bihac area. We see here Bihac, Celebici, Kamenica, Konjic, and it says Livno, Witness. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then Manjaca is mentioned under Livno. Under whose control was Manjaca at the time in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Manjaca was under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Correct. Then we come to Mostar. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And then it says Orasje and Rascani, Rodoc, and Tomislavgrad. So the towns and centres and areas are mentioned which pursuant to the order by Bruno Stojic the prisoners were released from. Can you tell me now, please, whether you remember at that time, and would you take a look at A, we see that it relates to Bihac. That's on the following page. A is Bihac, B is Celebici and Konjic. Now, in Konjic at that time, to the best of your recollections, is that where there were Croat detainees as well, as well as Serbs? So Serbs and Croats in Celebici and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, I don't want to go through the document. We have dealt with it. If Their Honours wish to ask a question they will do so, but anyway, all these areas and all three sides were duty-bound to comply and release the prisoners by a certain date. Is that what emerges from this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, at roughly at this period of time, and we see that the date is the 20th of October, 1992, have any knowledge that discussions were going on in Geneva about this topic, that is say the release of prisoners, and at the London conference, too, and was it usual and customary that after conferences of this kind these kind of conclusions would be made which were sometimes implemented, sometimes not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I see this document that you're showing to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm quite sure that you might have seen it when the Prosecutor showed you. I'm not asking you about that, but I'm asking you of whether you were are aware of conferences like this taking place and that usually after conferences of this type the detainees were released on the principle of all for all.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of that, but when the order came to release the prisoners we released them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Now, let's us take a look at another document -- or, rather, two documents on e-court. You commented on one of them and they are P 00514, or, that's the first one. It will appear on e-court. You won't find it in my binder because they are documents shown you by the Prosecutor. So I think the best thing to do is to wait until it appears on e-court. Here it comes. All I need is the title. It is "Instructions on the work of the central military prison of the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar," and you confirmed this. This set of instructions was brought on the 22nd of September, 1992. You said you received those instructions and acted upon them in Heliodrom. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: May we now have on e-court the following document: P 01474. That's also a document from the binder shown you by the Prosecutor, P 01474. Here. Look at this instruction. Have you seen it before? We don't need to go through all the pages. It's in part the house rules in centres for military prisoners and POWs issued on the 11th of February, 1993, and it says: "Director of the defence department, Bruno Stojic." Have you seen this? That's my only question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you say, "I haven't," does that mean you didn't even see it in the binder shown you by the Prosecution, or you didn't see it before, or you have never seen it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica. Ms. Nozica, I think it is not in that binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in binder 13 that we got from the Prosecutor, which also includes the previous document. I don't know in which way the Prosecutor presented evidence to you. Maybe -- it was all in binder 13 the way we got it from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, with due respect, we do not have if on the list and we do not have it in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can my learned friend help us, because I have it both on the list and in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not in binder 13, Your Honour. Binder 13 was revised and provided to counsel on Monday, and it's not in that binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is not a catastrophe and I will not make an issue, but I think, in honesty, you must be made aware if it is like this, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand what I was supposed to do. It was in my binder 13, and it was not taken out, and it's a document that the Honourable Judges have seen before a couple of days ago. If I may go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did the witness see this document before? Did you ever receive it in prison?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen it before. I'm seeing it now for the first time. I got it from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you review it in proofing with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I would now like to move to another subject that includes certain documents you spoke about before, your own documents or documents of Mr. Bozic that were made available to Mr. Bruno Stojic. In your testimony yesterday, you said that after learning that on the 6th of August, 1993, a commission was appointed, a five-member panel, to regulate the situation in prisons, and you were the fifth member. After learning that, on two occasions you informed Mr. Bruno Stojic that this commission never met. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you first tell me if you remember the date when you learned that the commission was established and that you were its fifth member?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two or three days after this date that is mentioned. It's in the decision that I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we agree that it's also in your diary?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were you also informed by Mr. Bozic of this? He also received that document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received it together on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you repeat -- I want to avoid objections. Can you repeat yourself through what letters and in what way did you inform Mr. Stojic that the commission had never met?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never informed Mr. Bruno Stojic that the commission was not operating. In fact, as the fifth member of the commission, since I never attended any meetings and without knowing whether the commission was working or not, I took the liberty as its fifth member to address myself to Mr. Bruno Stojic and inform him of the problems and what was going on in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is a bit different, but still it's a very precise explanation. You did inform him as a member of the commission because you thought you were entitled to, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in those letters to him, you did not state that the commission wasn't working because you didn't even know it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now see one document that you saw yesterday in e-court, P 06170. Let me remind you while the document gets into e-court. It's a report dated 27th October, 1993, signed by you. It's a report on the work of the commission for the release of prisoners. That was the name of the commission, isn't it? Here it is in e-court. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You remember this. You signed it at the end, and you confirmed that yesterday. I only want to have a look. In the first part of this report you state that you were appointed to that commission, and then you go on to complain about certain things or, rather, point out certain things that in your opinion were not quite all right; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is your document. You point out that there is a shortage of guards.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in the second part, which is not really important to me, you point out certain omissions and deficiencies in the release of certain prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude from what you wrote about the work of the commission one absolutely cannot conclude, and you did not have the intention, if I may suggest that, that you were informing Mr. Stojic that the commission wasn't operating.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you understood me well, and if I understood you well, I wrote this without ever knowing whether the commission was working or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What I'm asking is whether a reader of your letter could conclude from the way this letter is phrased that the commission was or was not working.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my letter, the way I wrote it, a reader could conclude that I'm not a part of that commission. I think that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It can't be clear enough if you are writing a report on the work of the commission for the release of prisoners. It's the very title, the subject of the letter. However, I want to deal with something else now. You mentioned yesterday -- and can we see page 2 in e-court now. You mentioned yesterday you delivered this document to Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, and to Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There it is. So you put Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, in the first place among addressees, and Mr. Bruno Stojic in the second place. Can we see that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You told the Court yesterday that you considered Mr. Tuta to be an advisor to Mr. Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I considered him as such. It was written on the doors of his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was it indeed?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at another document and I'll skip all the other questions because you've just explain your impression, that's a document from binder 13 again, 68 -- that is P 06844. I am just checking. It is in our binder 13, but we'll see it in e-court. Sir, this is a document of the 24th November, 1993. It says: "Crime prevention department of the military police centre Mostar." It says, "24th November, 1993. On the premises of the central military investigations prison in Mostar an interview was conducted with you, Mr. Josip Praljak, concerning the circumstances of handing out documentation from the prison for photocopying to meet the requirements of the police of the Convicts Battalion." Let remind you that this interview took place a little less than a month ago after that letter you addressed to Mr. Bruno Stojic and Mr. Mladen Naletilic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I can't remember it at all. Can you simplify it? With whom did I speak?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Perica Grujic wrote this record, and I'll remind you of some passages in this document. Frankly, I'm surprised because you just said you reviewed all the documentation. This one was also in binder 13. It concerns you, and it's surprising that you didn't notice it when you were reviewing all the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Nozica. For your information, it is not in our version of this binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution obviously submitted one version of the binders to you and another to us. I don't know what has been submitted to you, but we have a chart con testing of three parts. In the 13 -- in part 13 there are various documents including this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps I can assist. The binders that we put in this morning, as you may recall, did not include binder 13. We put in binders 1 through 12, which were the ones -- the additional binders -- bundles that we asked the witness to review plus binder 14 or bundle 14 which was his diary. Bundle 13 is a separate category. That was the working bundle of documents more closely familiar -- or similar to the ones we use with every witness. As often happens, in preparing the witness I -- a further selection was made because we knew we would not be able to get through all the material in the original bundle 13 over the course of the weekend, and a revised bundle 13 was put together and provided and sent to the Defence. So it could be in -- counsel maybe looked at something that was in the original bundle 13, but not in the bundle 13 that was provided to the witness in court, which explains a number of things. Number one, it explains some of the difficulty that counsel may be having, would also explain why the witness says he doesn't remember specifically looking at that -- to those particular documents because they were not particularly put to him. But I want to make it very clear that's an entirely different situation than bundles 1 through 12 or 14. Bundle 13 is a different animal altogether and was revised and provided to counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must say that is not true. We received yesterday from the Prosecution, on Monday at 11.00, a letter, and I'll see if my colleagues have it, saying that some documents from other bundles will be moved to binder 13. We were told that some documents would not be used, but we were not told which. Therefore, that is the information that we have. I'm very sorry about this indeed, and as soon as I complete my cross-examination -- could you please kindly look at it. If I may ask the usher to show the Chamber what the Defence teams have received. But since I have been put in a very embarrassing situation, after my cross-examination I will copy all my documents and submit them to the Chamber. I would have done it earlier had I known that the Prosecution hasn't done it. I thought it was natural for you to have all the documents that we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In any case, let us look at the ELMO and see what the Prosecution advised us yesterday. We see in the first part that some the materials would not shall used. And have a look, please, at the second paragraph, which says that some documents would be moved to bundle 13 from bundles 1, 5, 7, and 9. So in our minds it -- the material remained the same with certain shifts within the binders. We did not receive a revised list of documents from binder 13. It seems that the Prosecution provided that revised list to you but not to us, and we worked on 200 or 300 documents more because we thought they would be used, I must say. Maybe we can return this letter to Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, while it's on the ELMO. The letter is exactly consistent with what I said a moment ago. It's exactly what we communicated on Monday. There shouldn't be any confusion about that. It says specifically, "Some of the materials that were on the earlier exhibit list, bundle 13, will not -- will not be shown to him during his testimony while two additional documents will be shown. A revised exhibit is attached." And in our view it was attached when they got the emails, the very same e-mail for which it was attached to the Chamber it was the same e-mail that went to the Defence and that is the information I've been provided. If I'm proven to be wrong, I will be, but that was the information. So I -- I regret the situation that counsel finds herself in. I -- it's not the Prosecution's fault. The documents are supposed to be in e-court. We should be able to use them, and really, although it's unfortunate, I think to put all this and to cast this as some sort of fault on behalf of the Prosecution is really unfair and the document, the letter speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Instead of wasting time on procedural matters, let's gets to the heart of the matter. I prefer spending time looking at the document rather than explaining I made a mistake or not or whatever. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I stand by what I said, and also it will be my duty to provide the Trial Chamber with all the documents that I showed the witness which you were not able to find in your own binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, let's move to the heart of the matter, as His Honour has just said, and take a look at paragraph two. It says, "Mr. Stanko Bozic was absent from his office on business, so insight into SVIZ's documentation and answers were provided by the deputy warden of the prison in the following order," and it says under item 1: "In regard to photocopying documentation of the SVIZ Mostar, which the warden of the SVIZ provided for captain Reuf Ajanovic, a member of the conflicts battalion, on a written request signed by the commander of the Convicts Battalion, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, aka Tuta, Josip Praljak explained that in the Mostar SVIZ, Mr. Naletilic was respected as an advisor to the chief of defence, Mr. Bruno Stojic, and so believing he was entitled to the authority of the rank of chief they provided the requested documentation," and they were release orders, "(when he made his request in writing)." Do you remember that, Witness, now that I have read out this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as writing this is concerned, what you've just read out, I just cannot remember that the official conversation conducted by Perica Jukic and Grujic was as official as to be followed up by a report of this kind, so that actually I never read this report. What I want to say is this: Nobody ever asked me to make a statement of any kind let alone Perica Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, let's just clarify one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't going to intervene in order to save time, but I have to step in at this point because I'm looking at your diary, your logbook, where you have entries on what was going on, and for the 21st of November you mention the report that we have here, which is 2837/83, and you say that when the commission was established with the president, Mr. Pusic, you never met him. Now, you decided to inform us of certain important -- important events in prison. You inform Mr. Roso, Mr. Lavric, Mr. Jukic, and Mr. Bruno Stojic, and you also indicate: "I have since written a report to Mr. Stojic." Now, do you remember having written those entries in your diary about all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it says so in the diary, then I did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question, Mr. President. The president is, does he have an independent memory, as opposed to does the diary reflect that, and/or whether the diary refreshed his memory, not having one, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Mr. Usher, show the witness this page of his diary and his entry in it. We'll save time. Place it on the ELMO, please. On the ELMO so that we can all see it. Do you remember having written that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much, but I'd like to clarify this point, not to lead to a misunderstanding. I will come to that entry. And it is true that this witness wrote a report on that day, but I am talking about a conversation that took place on that same day according to this report that we have on e-court. It is P 06844, and it's the conversation that relates to Mr. Tuta. It just coincides by chance with the date when this witness actually wrote another report to Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, you said you made no statement. Sir, you also worked in the military police, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This isn't a statement, is it? So you and I can conclude that sometimes notes were written about certain events which took place and that those notes were Official Notes that you did not receive, but they were nonetheless compiled; is that right? Would things like that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you answer and tell me whether you remember this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the person, Perica Grujic, who otherwise I know personally. I don't remember him ever coming to me officially and that we discussed matters of this kind. That's what I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that there was any talk of taking out this document on the release that someone took pursuant to an order from Mr. Mladen Naletilic? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I can see here, the warden gave this at the time, that is to say Mr. Bozic, and that Mr. Perica Grujic came by to compile a report about that. So I probably, as it says here, explained this, gave explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also say, sir, that you respected -- am I right in saying that you respected the advisor of the defence department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, that is to say his advisor Mr. Naletilic? Now, look at what it says further on, that Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, to the SVIZ, did not use the memorandum of advisor of the defence department but on the memorandum of the Convicts Battalion. And Mr. Praljak had no answer to that, it says, and he explained everything hiding behind the authority of Mr. Naletilic as advisor to the chief. Do you remember that conversation and your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say to this day that what he was, was an advisor, and as such I respected him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, quite obviously from these documents we can see that Mr. Naletilic would send certain documents -- well, you said he never came by, but the Prosecutor showed you some documents, so tell me now, please, do you know that proceedings were taken against Mr. Naletilic in this Tribunal, and do you know that during that trial nobody ever established that he was an advisor to Mr. Bruno Stojic? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for the record, I'm not so sure -- I don't want to indicate any agreement with that statement. I'll have to he review the entire evidence in the Tuta-Stela case and the judgement. I just want to make sure that the Prosecution doesn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution is not testifying at this point. The witness is and that's an improper intervention by Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was responding to counsel's assertion. Not anything the witness said whatsoever but counsel's assertion of what was proved or not proved in the Tuta-Stela case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't think we'd have a debate over that. I didn't know Mr. Scott was a member of the Prosecution in the matter but I will leave that reservation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica, I'm trying to understand why you're asking these questions. Are you challenging the fact that Mr. Naletilic had an office next to Mr. Stojic and therefore if he was an advisor to Mr. Stojic it is quite normal that Mr. Praljak in going -- went to see the advisor rather than the big boss. That's normal. So is that what you're challenging? I don't quite understand where you're leading much perhaps you'll elucidate the point through another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Since you've asked me directly what I'm challenging, I'm challenging that Mr. Tuta was the advisor to Mr. Stojic, because up to now we have heard a series of witnesses, and I'm trying to establish through the witness where this respect for Mr. Naletilic comes from during that period of time, but I am not challenging - you asked me - I'm not challenging that Mr. Naletilic at a given period of time had an office on the same floor as Mr. Stojic, but he wasn't the only person who had an office on that floor and in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have heard all this and it's very clear now. The Stojic Defence and Mr. Stojic himself are challenging the fact that Mr. Naletilic was in fact an advisor to Mr. Stojic. What do you ever to say to that? What do you think? You met him. What do you -- what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I'm concern, at that time when I addressed him he was the advisor to Bruno Stojic for security matters with an office that was quite visible and clear, and he was sitting in the office himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, this question when I saw your report, you put that it was addressed to number one, Mr. Naletilic, and Mr. Stojic as number two. As a general rule one would do the reverse. We would -- you would generally put the most important person first and the other person underneath, whereas you reversed this order. The report is an official document. There's a number and so on. So when you sent out this report with Mr. Naletilic in number one place and Mr. Stojic, in your mind you were addressing it to the same entity, were you? That's what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It may be just a slip of the secretary that typed out the document, this report. She might have made a slip, that's all, because everyone knows that Mr. Bruno Stojic was the chief and Naletilic the advisor. So it could have been a slip on the typist's part. That's how I can explain it, the only way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I try to contribute to clarify this matter. You have said, Mr. Praljak, that on the office which was used by Mr. Naletilic it was written, "advisor to the minister of defence," or to Mr. Stojic. Was Mr. Naletilic's name used in this context, or is it possible that this was an office which was designated for an advisor of Mr. Stojic, but since Mr. Naletilic used this office but that would then not mean that he was an advisor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, what I know is that he was an advisor, and that's the only way I knew him and by the same token respected him in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to ask you one more thing. Did you ever see a single memorandum of Mr. Naletilic where it said that he was the advisor to Bruno Stojic? First of all, answer that question. Did you ever see a memorandum to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, because there was no reason for a memorandum to -- like that to come to the prison, and it didn't ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But a memorandum from the Convicts Battalion, whose commander Mr. Naletilic was, did come to you at the prison, did they not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean there the ATG Baja Kraljevic, their unit was put up at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I know that. From the previous document we saw that the prison did issue certain documents to one -- to a particular unit, but are you trying to justify that act by claiming before this Court that you considered Mr. Naletilic to be the advisor of Mr. Stojic and therefore justify yourself for having issued certain documents to the commander of some unit which was stationed at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, let's me tell you this, with all due respect: That document -- those documents were not issued by Josip Praljak but they were issued by Stanko Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I didn't say that. In the document it says it was issued by Stanko Bozic. What I'm saying is that the prison issued it, meaning the warden and deputy warden. You all worked together in the prison. But I won't belabour the point and insist upon an answer. I'm wasting time. Let me just deal with one more area raised by His Honour Judge Antonetti, the report of the 24th of November, 1993, which is recorded in your entry, in your diary, and the judge rightly said that you informed Mr. Stojic that the commission wasn't working, wasn't functioning. And we'd just like to take a look -- take a -- take a brief look at the report. It is P 068484, or, rather, 48, it was looked at yesterday and that's how I assume the Judges come to have it in their binders. And I'll end there. I'll get through this very quickly and bring my cross-examination to an end. Let's have a look at the document. It is a report of the 24th of November, 1993. You said that you addressed it to Mr. Stojic and that in your own handwriting you corrected the name of Bruno Stojic with Perica Jukic, because while writing the document you learnt that Mr. Stojic was no longer the head of the defence department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I don't want to deal with the whole document. Mr. Stojic didn't receive it, but it says in the first sentence, "as a member of the commission to establish greater order in prisons and otherwise authorised as set out in the order I would like to stress some highly important matters relating to the Mostar Heliodrom SVZ central military prison." So all I can ask you, sir, is in this sentence does it say where? It says the commission did not meet. And did you say at any time that the commission wasn't meeting and that that's why I was intervening? Do you agree that there is no mention of that in this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for clarification, you've said something like this before and it's important for me to get it right. We'll go through two documents from which we'll see until when Mr. Stojic occupied the position of chief of defence, and I think based on the documents that have been shown to you it's rather important. Can we see in e-court, and it's in front of you, sir, but still it will be on our screens, P 06583. 6583. Have you found it perhaps? It's a communique, a press release, signed by office of the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. For the benefit of the court and the Prosecution, it's in this binder. Yes. We see it in front us now. So, 10th November, 1993, and we see the names of the members of the new government. This is what this press release says. We see on this list a new Prime Minister and new deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We see Mr. Bruno Stojic. And another document 2D 00416, 2D 00416. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a protocol written on the 15th of November, for the record, 1993, and it says it was drafted on that day in Mostar with regard to the hand-over, takeover of duties between the hitherto minister of defence Mr. Bruno Stojic and the newly appointed minister of defence, Mr. Perica Jukic. We see the subject of this transition of duties, which doesn't matter to us at this moment. It was signed by both Mr. Bruno Stojic and Mr. Perica Jukic. Sir, does this tally with what you know, namely when you September that letter on the 24th November, 1993, that at that time Mr. Bruno Stojic was no longer chief of defence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know that. That's why I crossed out that name and wrote Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You confuse me now. What didn't you know?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I learned. That's when I crossed out Stojic's name and wrote in hand Perica Jukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm only asking you was it precisely at that time, seven or nine days after this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in conclusion, sir, I will ask you very briefly, we have another confusing thing in our documentation, and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, one clarification. In your diary for the 24th of 11th, 24th November, you didn't cross out Mr. Stojic. You crossed out Mr. Jukic. It must have been a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In conclusion, could we look at -- in the documentation that the Prosecution showed you in the past two days, we saw that you had a number of duties. You were warden in January, February, March, as you explained.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You signed one of the documents, and I'll say for the record it's P 04233, as deputy -- sorry, "assistant commander of the 5th Battalion of the military police - warden." Did you also use that title?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, never. I see it for the first time now. It must have been a slip paid by the secretary who wrote this. I never used that title.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But you were deputy warden, and you used that title on many occasions; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You also used the title, commander of the central military investigations prison, and signed documents that way?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in one period when it was necessary to achieve greater control over the guards service as ordered by Mr. Franjo Cvitkovic, then chief of the general military police at the administration. At that time I wrote that book, and I invoked the instructions that would be obeyed in handing over prisoners of war for labour duties, and in that period five to six men left the prison because they could not stand this tight a discipline. Among them was one man from the criminal service of the military police who was expelled, and another one was disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. My time is running out, and I don't want to be reprimanded by the Court. I want to finish. I conclude, and I believe my colleagues will deal with it at greater length, that Franjo Cvitkovic gave you certain authorisations, certain greater powers than normally in the possession of a deputy warden. Tell me, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long, because I talked to Franjo Cvitkovic in Ljubuski and told him that after all, I was appointed as a fifth member of that commission set up by Bruno Stojic, that it was too much, that I would have everything under control and everything would be all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Could that have been 10 days, not more?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could say that. But it was a long time ago you must bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On document P 04500, on the 25th of August you signed as deputy warden and chief of SIZ?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you receive any letters of appointment or was that verbal orders?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew I was deputy warden. That's how I signed it. But this signature is commander. That was part of these tighter control measures. I signed myself commander to make it sound better and to have greater effect on the security.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we conclude, sir, that all these titles that you used in signing various documents were used in fact in the period from the beginning of 1993 until the end of 1994? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we also agree that in actual fact you did not receive any letters of appointment at that time. Those appointments were given to you verbally or that you assumed according to the powers you had.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in your diary, 23rd May, 1994, you indicate that there was an order from Mr. Siljeg to Mr. Bozic asking for the transfer of his responsibilities to you, and the number of the order is 0211 something, and that's an order that appoints you officially director as of 18th May, 1994. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from that time on you were the only director, that is from end May 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that to correct Mrs. Nozica, who said that there was nothing until the end of 1994. There was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must have been a misunderstanding. I was talking about titles for the duration of 1993. Now that you ask this question about 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally I don't make any mistakes. In line 1 on page 71, you ask him about the period from the beginning of 1993 until the end of 1994. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now you tell me it's all 1993. Maybe you made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I said from the beginning of 1993 to the end of 1993, but I didn't see it before in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, Witness, when Honourable Judge Antonetti told you ago about your diary, at this point did you sign as deputy commander of the independent company of security? And I'm referring to document P 08241 of the 29th April, 1994, deputy commander of the independent security company KRZ. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that appointment from Mr. Siljeg on the 1st of January, 1994, and I was appointed deputy warden of that prison all the way until the time that the Judge mentioned. Then I became commander, but 20 days later the whole Heliodrom was closed down as a military prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, whether in 1994, on the 29th of April, you were deputy commander of the independent security company of the KRZ. That is your signature. Were you that too?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me finally about all these titles that you used when you signed documents, do they actually testify to the fact that you had rather wide powers within the Heliodrom prison in 1993? And, as we see, in the beginning of 1994. Is that your opinion as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such powers as you indicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't say what kind of powers you had. I'm talking about your titles and positions, the titles that you used. Did they give you the powers that go with these titles?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that whole 1993 I acted as indicated by the way I signed my name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That is the answer I expected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, there was a document that you did not show, 4455, that could have been interesting -- or 4475, that could have been interesting as a layout of the prison. You still have an opportunity to present it if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I had another two important documents, you just reminded me of one, and another one would have been rather important to me, the one from Mr. Bagaric, but unfortunately -- I wanted to conclude before you reprimand me, but since I've been given this opportunity by Honourable Judge, let us look at P 04475.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is an interesting schematic that you made on the 24th of August, 1993. I see that the Chamber is displaying some interest, and I'm interested in it too. Tell me, for what purpose was this done? You said it was done for peacetime, but you did it on the 24th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had worked for so many years in the prison system before the war, I made this schematic, this organisational chart, in order to assist the administration of military police, and at that time I think Mr. Rade Lavric was there, so that it could serve as a basis for the functioning of the prison in good security conditions. I never received a reply to this proposal, nor was it implemented, and later a different system was introduced and the centre for POWs was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two things I'm interested in, Witness. In this organigramme, in the B/C/S version because the English version is not quite the same, I'm interested in the relations between security commander and the warden. I see you put an arrow that goes from security commander to the director without going through you. Can you explain that? From the security commander to warden, bypassing you, because we see that the military policemen are divided in four groups led each by a lance corporal. These groups are answerable to the security commander, and that's why you drew an arrow showing up. However, there is no arrow between you and the security commander, only the warden and security commander. Is that a mistake? I don't think it's a mistake but, still, can you tell me in so many words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From experience, from my pre-war experience in the prison system, the warden of the prison could only -- were the only ones who could issue orders to the security commander. That's why I wrote that orders can issue only from the warden of the prison who is responsible for the whole prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Accepting the theory that you are an assistant commander or acting commander, acting commander, for instance, when you are standing in for the commander when he's absent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the second element for us to proceed speedily. There's a mention in this document that we're seeing for the first time and nobody has asked you that question, and I'm going to ask you that question now. It says "Remarks," and says the prison belongs to the military judiciary, and then you mention the president of the military court or tribunal. So apparently somebody we've never seen appears here, the president of the military tribunal or court. Now, this individual, did they come to the prison to see how it was functioning? Because it's probably a military court judge. So in any democracy in your country was a democracy at the time, military -- the military justice was interested in the prison system, and if this was written there then it corresponded to the actual situation. So do you remember the military prosecutor or the president of the military court ever coming to visit the prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I give an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is an organigramme compiled when most of the prisoners of war were being released, they focus on the prison building. That's what it refers to, where the only people that remain were military prisoners of war who at that time belonged to the military courts, military judiciary. I think it was Mr. Mladen Jurisic at the time who otherwise had the power and authority over the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to learn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have an additional question with regard to this same document. It is said there on the second page in the English version: "The most responsible worker is the warden and assistant warden, who is appointed by the judiciary." Can you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you explain why you wrote this here and why at least so far you have not with any indication said that you or Mr. Bozic were appointed by the judiciary? On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be of some assistance, Your Honour, prior to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: No. I think I would like to hear this from the witness and not from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you wait a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- it was a proposal, Your Honour. This was a proposal. He indicated -- I'm trying to assist you here. This was a proposal. He indicated this when he began being questioned about this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that's -- so perhaps you may wish to rephrase your question, but I'm not trying to interfere. He indicated that it was his proposal. So in light of that, there might be a line of questioning what existed prior to and what this proposal is about. So I apologise if I'm trying to interrupt, but I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I recognise your good intentions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I wanted to intervene in two matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Allow the witness to answer first, because Mr. Karnavas tried to explain the matter to the Chamber saying that the document was a proposal rather than a reality or, rather, I'm putting the word "reality" in there. But Mr. Praljak, who understands all this, will throw light on the matter. Now, Mr. Praljak, this document, it was an observation or a proposal to Mr. Rado Lavric, which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a proposal for Mr. Lavric so that the -- saying that the prison would function best in this way. So that was the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We took a bit of time up on that, but my only question was linked to this document, and it was why this document was compiled. At your own initiative because you thought this was the best way it would function, or did somebody ask you to compile something like this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me state again I felt it my moral duty as the fifth member to help things change, to make the prison a proper prison by virtue of its function, and for those reasons I made this proposal and sent it to Mr. Rado Lavric as food for thought, for him to think about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. You keep mentioning the fifth member, whereas you send it to Rado Lavric who wasn't a member of the commission at all and didn't work within the commission. So I think that in this context that rather sidesteps your -- or goes beyond your authority. But let me ask you one more thing. After moving to the organisation of the Konevcic [phoen], the shelter, was this proposal taken into account when the central military prison became the shelter of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received a response, but the book that -- for the book -- the system book for the prison incorporated this part here, as set out here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, do you mean to say that the prison came to belong to the military judiciary and was responsible to the president of the military court during 1994 after the reorganisation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It always belonged to the military police administration as an independent company, the shelter for prisoner of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have this next document in e-court, and Judge Antonetti noticed that the organigramme in the original does not correspond to the translation version. This is rather significant, and I think that if we're looking at this diagram then it is best to look at the original, of course, is it not, rather than the translation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you for that additional time, Your Honours. That completes my cross-examination, and I think it's time for the break as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going to take the break because it's 12.30. We have 20 minutes for our break and we will reconvene which will leave us with another hour to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The questions have two -- the Judges have two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: First -- first question, Mr. Praljak. It relates to document P 09121. I don't think it is necessary to show it to you. You will recall. It is this plan of the layout of Heliodrom, which is entitled inter alia "Concentration camp." Now, you have yourself personally taken a great distance and say you would not even want to pronounce that, but where does this document come from? Isn't it an official document which comes from -- I don't know from who. It speaks of JNA on the first line, but I don't know whether in B/C/S this also means -- has some meaning. Yugoslav National Army. I don't know. Can you give an explanation on the origin of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document on which it says "concentration camp" which we were shown earlier on by counsel, all I said was that I cannot accept the words "concentration camp" and I would never use those words myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I recall that very well, Mr. Praljak. My question was: Where does this document come from? It says "HVO concentration camp."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You had never seen it before today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I was shown by counsel, I marked on it the prison on the Heliodrom premises where the prisoners were kept, but I didn't deal with what it says at the top, where it says they were concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you wanted to explain, Ms. Nozica. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that we can explain it quite simply if we just ask the witness whether it was the Prosecutor who showed him the document, and then when he talked to the Prosecutor on the 16th of March, 2004, the document had already been prepared by the Prosecutor and then he made these markings in his own hand on the document. I think that the witness can tell us that and then the origins of the document will be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was either the Prosecutor who gave you this map or you brought it with you when you met with the Prosecutor. Which was it? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigators. When the investigators talked to me, they showed me that document. I did not pay any attention to what it says in the capital letters above at the top of the document. I just looked at the Heliodrom compound and marked the premises where the prisoners of war and prisoners were detained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, would you inform the Chamber where the document originates from? Was it your services who wrote this up, or did you get the document from somewhere else, because it has to have come from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Mr. President and Your Honours, I was looking for the document because I had it out, the one that was actually used with the witness in court earlier this -- on Monday, and I had it a few minutes ago before the break but ... Here it is. I have it. First of all, just to explain, I believe the document was shown to the witness when he was interviewed in 2004 as he himself has just confirmed, there was no reference to the title on the document, and the Prosecution made no effort to make any use of that, if you will. It was a document that was found -- it was an existing -- a pre-existing diagram of the Heliodrom complex that was used for the diagram itself having nothing to do with the title of the document, for -- something for the witness to mark. When it was used with the witness in court, IC number 449, if anyone would like to look at it just so that they can confirm what I'm telling is the truth. The part didn't have anything on that. It simply was that particular section of it that showed the -- the part of the prison complex. It had nothing to do -- we didn't use anything -- any other markings on the document, but it indeed was shown to the witness as a -- something for him to mark on in 2004. That's all. That's the only information I can provide to the Chamber at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Do you have in your possession the document marked P 09121?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Because that is the one I was referring to. Ms. Nozica is offering you a copy. Perhaps the usher can bring it over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's the one we're talking about, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But this one has the title, and the other one you held up does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps you weren't listening and didn't hear what I said. This was shown to the witness in 2004 by the investigators when the witness was interviewed in 2004, not in court on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's what I just said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know offhand. I'd have to do some further inquiries to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do your best to find out, because it's important for us to know where the document comes from, and then you'll tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The second question, Mr. Praljak, is did you personally visit the solitary confinement cells that we have spoken about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once or twice at the most throughout that entire period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would that have been before or after the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the time after the 30th of June. From the 30th of June onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel, next team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak. I am Defence counsel for General Praljak, and I have a few questions for you, not too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honours, I will complete my cross-examination within 10 minutes, and we give the rest of our time to the Pusic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, tell me, please, did you ever see General Praljak in the Heliodrom complex?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that General Praljak had come to the complex?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you knew more or less the entire complex, and Their Honours have had occasion to see photographs. It's a large complex, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Within that Heliodrom complex, was there a cinema hall as well?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us without having to resort to photographs, although we can if need be, where was the cinema hall located? Was it a long way off from the detention centre, the detention building, or what?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't quite remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, shall we take a look on e-court the layout. It was P 09219. Perhaps we could place that on the overhead projector or on e-court -- on e-court. It is a layout. It was IC 452, because the witness marked the detention building. So may we have that on e-court. It had an IC number being 452. Until that comes up on our screens let me ask you this: Do you know where the canteen was, once again, in the complex, the officers' mess or officers' canteen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether that building where the canteen was, whether it was near the detention building or a long way away or where?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is separated by the command building to the south where the command was, and next to that was the canteen or officers' mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you take a look at your screen, because the layout, the diagram of the entire complex has come up on our screens, and could you point out to us --.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the usher's assistance so that the witness can mark with a marker pen where this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us where the prison building was. You already marked that. Or the main building, main prison building, the one that you reconstructed. And you can draw a circle around that.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And put a number 1 there, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excellent. Now, on this diagram can you recognise the cinema building?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I know there was a cinema building there but I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know what building it was in?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I would make a mistake if I were to hazard a guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, could you give us the general area where the cinema might have been?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you say that it was to the left or right of the stadium or the prison or do you have any idea whatsoever where the cinema hall might have been?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a kitchen. I know where the kitchen was, the central kitchen where we had our meals, and above us was the Bruno Pusic regiment. That's the area that I moved around in and knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you can't actually say, can you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the canteen? Can you locate that for us, please -- or, rather, the building where the canteen was.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And would you put a number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it true and correct, in looking at this diagram, if I say between the prison building and the canteen building there was a building in between the two? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, would the witness put his initials in the margin at the bottom and today's date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The date is the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may I have an IC number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC number, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC 453, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We don't need the document any more. Thank you, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Their Honours asked you when you came in as a witness whether you were related to General Praljak, and you said yes you were, that you were cousins; start?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So undoubtedly you know each other. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever during the war, during the war we're discussing, personally meet General Praljak during that time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once at the annual celebrations of the military police in Ljubuski -- Ljubusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that was in actual fact after the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the war and especially in 1992 and 1993 when you worked at Heliodrom, did you ever happen to meet him then?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have the usher's assistance and place on the e-court document P 06937.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, this morning at the beginning of the day when you were asked by the Prosecutor, you confirmed that you had seen all the documents in the binder and therefore testified to the authenticity of the documents. You know what I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you now take a look at this next document up on our screens and tell me whether in that binder where reference is made to the group of orders signed by Jelic, whether this document is among that group in that binder?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I went through the documents rather quickly, and I said that it was in the order it was, I didn't happen to notice this particular one. And I see that at the bottom there's an addition -- an additional part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you cannot confirm that you have seen this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In that case, I only have one more question, because it's of no importance then. This document seems to me a little unusual judging by its form since there are two stamps and two signatories. Now, any of the other documents from this category of orders from Mijo Jelic, do you remember whether there was any other document with two signatures and two stamps?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I happened to notice one from General Petkovic, and I think that I also saw one from General Matic like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on the following: As a rule, all the documents have a signatory -- or, rather, one person who signs and one stamp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So exceptionally, and you now told us two examples that you remember, for some reason you remember documents with two signatories and two stamps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember this particular one?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that you've never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, with respect to the stamps, I see that there were prison stamps and that there was a number 47 on them when we saw the prison stamps. Now, one could ask ourselves whether your signature is followed by a stamp as well because we can't see the number 7. Is it your signature underneath Mr. Jelic's signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what name is it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zlatan Mijo Jelic. And underneath that in handwritten form is says "Slobodan Praljak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So in your opinion, what was Mr. Praljak's part in this document or in this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this time there was an order prohibiting prisoner of war from being released to perform labour. They could only do so with permission from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just to -- add to your last questions, Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Praljak, can you affirm that you have not seen this document in the many, many documents that you have been shown? Can you say it's excluded, "I would certainly have noticed and remembered this one"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, skimming through that document I don't think I saw this document, but I saw similar documents from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. It says 8th November at 2120. Is this something you wrote yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it's somebody at the prison who must have marked it. Somebody left or came back at 2120.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who wrote this was an officer of the guards or maybe shift commander who was on duty then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's an entry made at the prison. So at that time, as you said, you were never there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just now -- in fact, no. I want to ask you something else. After telling us you don't remember seeing this document over the weekend in the Prosecutor's office, do you remember seeing it at the time of the events, on the 9th of November, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And let me go back to the following: As you were questioned by the Bench a moment ago, an order was mentioned, the order of General Petkovic dated 14th November, 1993, banning the prisoners from being borrowed, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And after that we saw many orders contrary to Mr. Petkovic's order, and we see documents to the effect that prisoners continued to be taken out, and such orders continued. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This one is dated 8th of November. That is between the order of Mr. Petkovic and this order there is a whole series, at least a dozen, which tells us that orders continued to come in from Mijo Jelic, among others, and they continued to be implemented. It didn't take anybody superior to Jelic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this order was obviously executed, at least according to this entry. This one was executed as well regardless of whether it had two signatures and two stamps or just one; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we heard what the witness said, and regardless of all the technology we have at our disposal here when the Prosecutor enters this document I will object, and immediately for the record I want to say this document is a forgery. The witness does not remember seeing it at the time. He doesn't recall seeing it even recently at the Prosecutor's office. And I want to remind the Chamber that as was established in previous cases this document was indeed obtained from the Croatian archives, but what both we and the Prosecution received at the archives are only copies. And I remind the Court of a well-known fact that the chain of custody of HVO documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia took five years, and in those five years the documents were in the possession of at least three different intelligence services. Therefore, I believe, and that is a rare occurrence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
