utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, to be quite clear, you seem to maintain that the signature is not that of Mr. Praljak, because -- because it's a forgery. Is that what you're saying? Is that a false signature? I'm trying to understand what you're saying, because apparently this document has a reference number, dates, numbers. All that is established. There is a stamp or stamps. We see a handwritten addition, 8th November, 2120. Then we see a stamp of receipt with a reference number 412. Then we see the signature of Mr. Praljak. So are you saying that this is all a forgery?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to explain in greater detail. I had to mention the issue of the chain of custody just to remind you of that story and that fact stands. It has been established in other cases. I'm not claiming the whole of the document is a forgery but still it is false. Because according to our information, and that can be proven only by expertise for which purpose I will ask the Prosecution for an original, I think that this little square at the bottom was simply pasted during photocopying, and I think we can see the outlines of that pasted square even with the naked eye. It was simply added to another document. Since we are working with copies here and copies are mostly fine, they are mostly verifiable, we usually have three copies from various archives, the archives of the issuing institution, archives of the receiving institution, and some third source, it's usually easily verifiable. However, despite all our efforts we were able to find this document only in the Croatian archives, but we do not know the chain of custody of this document before it reached the Croatian archives. In those five years of its journey, anybody could have pasted this addition at the bottom. In any case, I just wanted to lay briefly a foundation, and our in our written submissions tomorrow I will explain further and object because this document is not authentic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But so that I understand what you're saying, of course you can paste a stamp, but you have a signature as well here. You know we can have a graphological examination, and it can well be established that it is indeed your client's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a problem to take from another document an original signature of Mr. Praljak or any other person and -- and the stamp that accompanies it. Only this bit can be pasted onto another document and then the whole can be copied, Xeroxed. We are not being paranoid here. Although we have to handle thousands of copies, in 99.9 per cent of cases those copies are verified and verifiable. This is not the case here. Of course, this document can be submitted to expertise only when we have an original. Our inquiries did not yield an original. The Prosecution has a copy from the Croatian archives and so do the Defence teams. That's all we have. But I will inquire further and see what the chances are that Mr. Praljak really signed this document on the 8th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, the Prosecution questioned you about this as well, and I have to follow up on that. Do you know that General Praljak -- in fact, do you know from any source at all, firsthand or secondhand, that General Praljak was relieved of his duties as commander at his own request on the 8th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In any case, you know that General Roso was commander after Praljak?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know maybe from other people or any other source or information that General Praljak on that day, the 8th of November, 1993, in the morning spent several hours in Citluk with Mr. Bruno Stojic whose underling you were after all? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the rest of the same day, the 8th of November, 1993, was spent by General Praljak in the process of handing over duties until late evening hours in Livno? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything at all about the movements of General Praljak on that day of hand-over of duties or earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now that we have discussed this document at length, was your memory jogged, perhaps? Did you see that document contemporaneously in 1993? I suppose you would have remarked the signature of your cousin.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, 1993, and I didn't even need to look at these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my cross-examination. I stand by what I said regarding the dubious authenticity of this document. Later in the process of proving an alibi I will show that Mr. Praljak was not even Mostar at the time, but I do also insist that we get the original document from the OTP, if they have it, so that we can submit it for expertise. But I believe that authenticity's very questionable. The witness says that he didn't see it at the time, which sounds reasonable, but he also says he didn't even see it during proofing in the past three days. The witness will, though, confirm that he had seen 100 documents in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, my apology to counsel for interrupting but I was going to get up before counsel started the next question. Just so the record is clear, there is no evidence in the record at the moment that this document is not authentic and counsel's assertions to the contrary are not evidence. So there's simply no evidence that it isn't authentic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this comment is really not appropriate. If there were any doubts on the Prosecution's side about the authenticity of this document I suppose they wouldn't be presenting it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you submit your arguments in writing, the Trial Chamber will confer and deliberate on the admissibility of this document, and you can trust us to review it as we normally do, very carefully, and with even greater care. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I will be very brief and cover three subjects. Just a little clarification concerning the order of my client, Mr. Petkovic, dated 14th October, 1993, document P 05881 that we discussed a moment ago. Can we please see it in e-court? And you, Mr. Praljak, would you be see kind as to look at your screen. I just want to ascertain the precise meaning of this document and avoid any confusion. Tell me, this is a document that General Petkovic issued to all the brigades of the operation zone of East Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it is a document that was not submitted either to Heliodrom prison or any other detention centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was submitted to the prison, and I found about it at the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's not so important whether the document reached Heliodrom in any way, but the author of the document did not actually intend it for any -- anyone but the brigades of the South-east Herzegovina operation zone. That much is true.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It says: "I hereby prohibit prisoners to be taken out for the purpose," et cetera. Now, tell me, is it correct to interpret this order as an order of the Main Staff to brigades in the operation zone prohibiting them from even requesting prisoners for any purpose without the approval of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I didn't follow the interpretation, but I hope that everything's properly on the record. The next topic are the women you said were at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private is session, please, to mention some names?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, this question about the women was very important to me because of an order issued by my client, General Petkovic, dated the 30th of June, 1993, whereby he issues the order for the isolation and disarmament of Muslims in the HVO and also the isolation of the military-able men with the express order not to touch the women and children. Tell me, please, do you know what happened on the 30th of June, 1993 in Mostar and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know what was going on because I wasn't living in Mostar at all, nor did I know what was happening in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll tell you briefly. The HVO in Mostar lost control over certain facilities and territory because the Muslims from the HVO crossed over to the side of the BH army and in that way betrayed their army, and that is why the order was issued, to isolate Muslims in the HVO. Tell me, Mr. Praljak, do you know that at the beginning of -- of July at Heliodrom Muslims were brought in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Counsel. They betrayed their own army, their army. Which army?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army they were in, and they were in the HVO right up until the point in time -- while somebody is in an army, then that is that person's army to which he belongs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, did you know that at Heliodrom at the beginning of July Muslims were brought in who were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Praljak, let's discuss categories, the categories of people who were deprived of liberty and taken in remand. You very often use the term "prisoners of war." Tell us, please, do you know who enjoys protection under that category according to the provisions that apply to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners of war, as I understand it, were those persons who were captured on that day, the 30th of June, and who began to be brought in to the Heliodrom on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me tell you briefly. There are several categories of prisoners of war, but basically a prisoner of war is a member of a hostile army, an enemy army, and various arms grouped to that or to them. That is a simplified version of the definition of a prisoner of war. Now, tell me, please, the persons of Muslim ethnicity who had been soldiers of the HVO, did they belong to that enemy army, and did these -- can these persons be considered prisoners of war in conformity with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you explain that to me, your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, if -- or, let's put it this way, give a specific time and place: Can soldiers of the BH army and the army of Republika Srpska with which the HVO at that time was engaged in a conflict be considered prisoners of war? And HVO prisoners of war armies -- soldiers of that same HVO?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prisoners of war from those two components are, as far as we were concerned, prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, what about HVO soldiers who were brought to Heliodrom regardless of their ethnicity? What status did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time when they were brought in to prison we did not know, although they were Muslims, whether they were in the HVO units or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us then, Mr. Praljak, and can you confirm, Mr. Praljak, that in the facilities that you mentioned, that is to say the prison, the school, and the sports hall that there were both HVO soldiers there who were Muslims and soldiers of the BH army and perhaps some third category of persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If from today's advantage point you were to try to establish who was taken out to perform labour according to the regulations, could you establish whether it was HVO soldiers who had been detained on the 30th of June and after that period?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I did not know at the time anything about this, I just learnt who the prisoners of war were when a criminal report was filed against these persons and when they were transferred to the prison building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when you received requests and demands to release prisoners to perform labour or detainees to perform labour, did you need to contact the administration of the detention centre? Did the administration of the detention centre have to see about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the order to release these people came, the shift commander did not differentiate between persons. He did not differentiate the different categories, but they would take these persons from prison out in a set order.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel Tomic, what do you want to tell us, because we have four minutes left? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would use these -- or, rather, two of those four minutes for some technical matters, not to waste time tomorrow. The Pusic Defence has told me that they won't be needing the time they were allotted by the Praljak Defence, so I would like to know how much the Praljak Defence has used up and how much time I have at my disposal. If you could tell me that today, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We said that Mr. Pusic has one hour and a half. That's what we started off with. Now, I understood it this way, that Mr. Pusic's Defence was given 30 minutes from that time, that Mr. Praljak's Defence gave Mr. Pusic 30 minutes, which means that Mr. Pusic has two hours. What I don't know is how much time Mr. Karnavas is going to need for the Prlic defence. Tomorrow, Mr. Karnavas, how much time are you going to need? You have 45 minutes in the natural order of things, but how much time are you going to need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to reserve my entire 45 minutes. I don't know if I will use it all, but at this point in time I'm not willing to give my time to anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make things clear for the transcript. We feel that one and a half hours accorded to us is sufficient. That will suffice us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You will need one and a half hours, and if we add to that the 45 minutes for the Prlic Defence, that is two hours and 15 minutes, plus -- well, you have Mr. Coric's time, which is one hour and 30 minutes, as you said, plus the time remaining, unless the Prosecution has additional questions, re-examination. Do you, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think there will be some, Your Honour. Based on what I've heard today, I have to at least allow for the possibility to reserve some time for some questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A priori, Mr. Scott, if you take too much we won't be able to get through everything in view of the fact that Counsel Ibrisimovic needs one hour and 30 minutes. Mr. Prlic needs 45 minutes, and we have a minimum of two hours for the Coric Defence, which means that that is a little over four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't use for -- first of all to start, I did not use all the time allocated to me to begin with, so we finished shorter than we thought. I will -- I'm certainly sensitive to the time issues just as everyone, I think, in the courtroom is, but having said that I cannot simply say as a matter of principle that I have no redirect. There may be some very important questions to put to the witness and I think it's the Prosecution's right, just as the right of every party, to pose its questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as we're going to have a meeting later on, the Judges, we will see about that and tell you how we're going to divide the time up tomorrow, but we have taken note of the request made by the Coric Defence to have more time. Well, you'll have your time, because you already have allocated to you one hour and 30 minutes, but we'll let you know tomorrow. The object, as far as we are concerned, is to ensure that Mr. Praljak can go home after the end of business tomorrow, not have to stay on, and I think we'll reach a consensus on that point. It's quarter to 2.00. We have to end that point. We reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
